t: Determine the Minimum Sum of a k-avoiding Array
o: Pick n distinct positive integers, no two distinct elements summing to k, minimizing the total. Greedy: take 1, 2, 3, ... skipping any x whose complement k−x is already taken. Small numbers 1..⌊k/2⌋ are mutually safe; after exhausting them, jump to k, k+1, ... which only pair with numbers below k that we avoided. Example: n=5, k=4 → [1,2,4,5,6], sum 18.
k: Numbers 1..⌊k/2⌋ never conflict with each other, so take them all first (or fewer if n is small).
Once past ⌊k/2⌋, start at k: k+x > k for x ≥ 1... precisely, values ≥ k only conflict with values < k, which were skipped, so k, k+1, ... are all safe.
Closed-form arithmetic series gives O(1); simulation gives O(n + k).

a.n: Approach 1: Greedy Simulation with a Set
a.i: Simulate the greedy directly: try x = 1, 2, 3, ...; accept x if k − x is not already chosen. This naturally implements 'take 1..⌊k/2⌋ then k, k+1, ...'.
s: Maintain a used set and running sum.
For x = 1, 2, ...: if k − x ∉ used, accept x until n values are chosen.
a.t: O(n + k) — x advances at most to about k + n

a.i: Take h = ⌊k/2⌋ smallest-safe numbers 1..h. If n ≤ h the answer is n(n+1)/2. Otherwise take all of 1..h (sum h(h+1)/2) plus t = n − h numbers starting at k: k, k+1, ..., k+t−1, summing to t·k + t(t−1)/2.
s: Compute h = k // 2, t = n − h.

w: Simulation is easiest to explain and prove; the formula is a nice optimization to mention. Pitfall: the boundary at ⌊k/2⌋ — for even k, k/2 pairs with itself but elements must be distinct, so k/2 is safe to include (h = ⌊k/2⌋ handles this correctly). Follow-up: k-avoiding with maximum sum, or with exactly n elements under an upper bound.
